metadata.name: Ecodesign for SQL and PL/SQL
metadata.description: Ecodesign rules for SQL and PL/SQL: sober reads, indexes and sargability, set-based processing, data lifecycle.

lectures.name: SQL — sober reads
lectures.description: Read and transfer only the rows and columns you need (RGESN Backend, GR491_Backend_1).

rules.title: SELECT * exposed
rules.description: Transfers every column, including the ones never read: network, memory and serialisation wasted, and breakage on the slightest schema change.
rules.recommendation: List explicitly the columns the need requires.

example.good: SELECT id, client_id, total FROM commandes;

rules.title: OFFSET pagination
rules.description: OFFSET reads and discards every skipped row: the cost of page N grows with N.
rules.recommendation: Cursor or keyset pagination: WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n.

rules.title: Non-sargable predicate
rules.description: A function applied to the filtered column (UPPER, DATE, CAST), or a LIKE '%...' with a leading wildcard, rules out the index: full table scan.
rules.recommendation: Rewrite the predicate against the raw column (a date range, a direct comparison) or create a dedicated functional index.

rules.title: SELECT DISTINCT hiding a join
rules.description: A DISTINCT added to remove duplicates usually hides an incorrect join: the database sorts or hashes the whole result for nothing.
rules.recommendation: Check the cardinality of the joins; prefer EXISTS over IN (subquery) on large volumes.

rules.title: Missing index on filtered columns
rules.description: A frequent WHERE, JOIN or ORDER BY clause with no index triggers a full scan on every execution.
rules.recommendation: Check the execution plan; index the frequently filtered columns, without duplicating an existing index (each one costs on every write).

ecritures.name: SQL — writes and processing
ecritures.description: Work set-based and in slices rather than row by row (RGESN Backend/Architecture).

rules.title: Row-by-row processing (cursor or loop)
rules.description: A cursor, or a loop issuing one statement per row, multiplies context switches and round trips where a single set-based statement would do.
rules.recommendation: UPDATE ... WHERE, INSERT ... SELECT or MERGE in one statement; failing that, BULK COLLECT (with LIMIT) and FORALL in PL/SQL.

example.good: UPDATE t SET x = 1 WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM t);

rules.title: COMMIT per row
rules.description: One COMMIT per row multiplies journal writes; conversely a giant transaction holds locks and undo.
rules.recommendation: COMMIT in sized batches (a few thousand rows), with bounded transactions.

rules.title: Mass delete or purge in a single statement
rules.description: A DELETE with no WHERE and no slicing saturates the journal, holds long locks, and can fail the whole operation.
rules.recommendation: Purge in chunks with pauses; consider TRUNCATE or partitioning where the semantics allow.

rules.title: Row-by-row logging in production
rules.description: DBMS_OUTPUT, or one log line per row inside a production loop, consumes CPU and storage for information nobody reads.
rules.recommendation: Log in batches or at the end of the job; keep production levels sober.

cycle_de_vie.name: SQL — data lifecycle
cycle_de_vie.description: Store less, and plan the end of life from the moment you create it (RGESN 7.3, GR491_Architecture_3/5).

rules.title: Oversized types by default
rules.description: VARCHAR(MAX) and CLOB "just in case" inflate storage, backups and transfers for the whole lifetime of the table.
rules.recommendation: Size the types to the real need (no BIGINT when INT is enough, no TEXT by default).

rules.title: No retention policy
rules.description: A table with neither purge nor archiving grows indefinitely: storage, backups and query times all increase without end.
rules.recommendation: Define retention and purge at creation time; plan partitioning or archiving for fast-growing tables.
